proofs.proof_tex:
By the covariate nondegeneracy assumption, there is an even deterministic index \(N_x\) such that \(\lambda_{\min}(S_{xx,n})\ge c_x/2\) for every even \(n\ge N_x\).  Likewise, residual nondegeneracy gives an even \(N_s\) such that \(v_n\ge c_s/2\) for every even \(n\ge N_s\).  On this tail \(S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}\) exists and has operator norm at most \(\sqrt{2/c_x}\), while \(s_n=\sqrt{v_n}\ge\sqrt{c_s/2}>0\).

Apply the complete-randomization vector central limit lemma to the first \(k\) coordinates of the score.  Its maximal-term condition follows from uniform boundedness and the preceding inverse bound:
\[
 \max_{i\le n}\frac{\|S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}x_{ni}\|^2}{n}
 \le \frac{2K_0^2}{c_x n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus \(D_n(W_{n,0})\Rightarrow G\).  Since the boundary of \(\{d:\|d\|^2\le a\}\) has \(G\)-probability zero,
\[
 p_n=\Pr\{\|D_n(W_{n,0})\|^2\le a\}
 \longrightarrow \Pr\{\|G\|^2\le a\}>0.
\]
Consequently \(p_n>0\), and hence \(\mathcal A_n(a)\ne\varnothing\), on a further deterministic even tail.  The three eventual properties in the definition of \(N_0\) therefore hold simultaneously, so the set over which its minimum is taken is nonempty and \(N_0<\infty\).

It remains to prove absorption rather than assume it.  The balanced pair-transposition graph is finite and connected: if \(w,w'\in\mathcal A_n\), successively interchange an index in \(\{i:w_i=1,w'_i=0\}\) with one in \(\{j:w_j=0,w'_j=1\}\).  At an exterior state \(M_n(w)>a>0\), every proposed neighboring transposition has strictly positive transition probability.  Indeed, an improving move is accepted, and a worsening move with positive finite score is accepted with probability \((M_n(w)/M_n(w^*))^\gamma>0\); a proposal with \(M_n(w^*)=0\) is accepted by definition.  Because the graph is finite and \(\mathcal A_n(a)\ne\varnothing\), from every exterior state there is a path of at most \(\#\mathcal A_n-1\) positive-probability transitions into \(\mathcal A_n(a)\).  Taking the minimum of the finitely many corresponding path probabilities gives \(\rho_n>0\).  By the Markov property, the probability of avoiding the target for \(r(\#\mathcal A_n-1)\) proposals is at most \((1-\rho_n)^r\), which tends to zero.  Hence \(T_n<\infty\) almost surely for each retained row.  This proves every assertion, and the finitely many discarded rows have no asymptotic role.

The score definition and covariate centering give
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^n d_{ni}=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n r_{ni}=0.
\]
The projection normal equations give \(S_{dr,n}=0\).  Moreover,
\[
 S_{dd,n}=S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}S_{xx,n}S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}=I_k,
 \qquad S_{rr,n}=s_n^{-2}v_n=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n q_{ni}q_{ni}^{\mathsf T}=I_{k+1}. \tag{1}
\]
Uniform boundedness, the lower eigenvalue bound, and \(s_n\ge\sqrt{c_s/2}\) imply \(\max_i\|q_{ni}\|\le C\) on the retained tail for a deterministic \(C<\infty\).  In particular \(n^{-1}\max_i\|q_{ni}\|^2\to0\).  The complete-randomization vector central limit lemma applied to (1) now yields
\[
 Z_n(W_{n,0})=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(2W_{n,0,i}-1)q_{ni}
 \Rightarrow \mathcal N_{k+1}(0,I_{k+1}).
\]
For reference, the covariance is exactly the identity: balanced sampling gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(2W_i-1,2W_j-1)=-1/(n-1)\) for \(i\ne j\), and centering plus (1) gives \(\operatorname{Var}\{Z_n(W_{n,0})\}=I_{k+1}\).

For the causal identity, fixed potential outcomes and equal allocation imply, for every \(w\in\mathcal A_n\),
\[
 \widehat\tau_n(w)-\tau_n
 =\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2w_i-1)\{Y_{ni}(1)+Y_{ni}(0)\}
 =\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2w_i-1)(h_{ni}-\bar h_n),
\]
where the last equality uses \(\sum_i(2w_i-1)=0\).  The score construction gives the exact projection identity
\[
 h_{ni}-\bar h_n=b_n^{\mathsf T}d_{ni}+s_nr_{ni}.
\]
Substitution, followed by taking \(w=W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}\), proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)
 =b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})+s_nE_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})
\]
without an approximation or a superpopulation argument.

Use the smooth extension from the resolved characteristic theorem and denote its original-proposal-clock interpolation by \(X_n(t)\).  It agrees with the original score process up to \(T_n\).  Its limiting drift and covariance are
\[
 \beta_\phi(d,e)=(-4d-8\gamma\phi'(\|d\|^2)d,-4e),
 \qquad c_\phi=8I_{k+1}. \tag{10}
\]
The all-pairs inverse-clock lemma is essential here: its success probability tends to \(1/2\), so it converts the half-speed auxiliary characteristics into exactly (10), not into a stationary-chain clock.

We first prove compact containment from the primitives.  The exact raw moments (5), the global Lipschitz bound for \(U\), and \(1-A\le Cn^{-1/2}\) imply
\[
 n\,\mathbb E\{\|X_{n,(m+1)/n}\|^2-\|X_{n,m/n}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_{n,m}\}
 \le C_1-c_1\|X_{n,m/n}\|^2 \tag{11}
\]
for constants \(C_1<\infty,c_1>0\) and all large \(n\).  To see (11), the raw drift contributes \(-8\|X\|^2\); the rejection correction is at most \(C\|X\|\), the raw quadratic term is bounded by \(C(1+\|X\|^2/n)\), and \(C\|X\|\le2\|X\|^2+C^2/8\).  Stopping (11) on first exit from a ball of radius \(R\), summing through \(nL\) steps, and using \(\mathbb E\|X_n(0)\|^2=k+1\) gives
\[
 \sup_n\Pr\left\{\sup_{t\le L}\|X_n(t)\|>R\right\}
 \le\frac{k+1+C_1L}{R^2}. \tag{12}
\]

On a ball of radius \(R\), the predictable drift and quadratic-variation rates are bounded, while the maximal jump is \(O(n^{-1/2})\).  The martingale decomposition and conditional second-moment bound therefore imply that, for stopping times \(\sigma_n\le L\) and deterministic \(\delta_n\downarrow0\),
\[
 X_n((\sigma_n+\delta_n)\wedge L)-X_n(\sigma_n)\longrightarrow_{\Pr}0
\]
after stopping at radius \(R\).  Letting \(R\to\infty\) using (12) proves tightness and continuity of all subsequential limits.

For \(f\in C_c^3(\mathbb R^{k+1})\), Taylor's formula and the jump bound give, uniformly before compact exit,
\[
 \begin{split}
 &\mathbb E\{f(X_{n,(m+1)/n})-f(X_{n,m/n})\mid\mathcal F_{n,m}\}\\
 &\quad=\nabla f(X_{n,m/n})^{\mathsf T}\mathbb E(\Delta Z_{n,m}\mid\mathcal F_{n,m})
 +\frac12\nabla^2f(X_{n,m/n}):\mathbb E(\Delta Z_{n,m}\Delta Z_{n,m}^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_{n,m})+O(n^{-3/2}).
 \end{split} \tag{13}
\]
The trajectory-uniform characteristic theorem makes the sum of the characteristic errors in (13) over \(m\le nL\) converge to zero in probability; bounded localization upgrades this to the martingale identity in every subsequential limit.  Thus each limit solves the martingale problem with generator
\[
 \mathcal L_\phi f=\beta_\phi^{\mathsf T}\nabla f+4\operatorname{tr}(\nabla^2f). \tag{14}
\]
The map \(\beta_\phi\) is globally Lipschitz: \(\phi\) is constant near zero and equals \(\log m\) away from zero, with a smooth compact transition.  Picard iteration gives a pathwise unique solution to the constant-diffusion stochastic equation associated with (14), and applying the usual Gronwall estimate to two solutions driven by the same Brownian motion proves uniqueness in law.  The initialization lemma identifies its initial law as independent standard Gaussian coordinates.  Hence every subsequence has the same limit.  Its coordinates solve
\[
 dD_t=(-4D_t-8\gamma\phi'(\|D_t\|^2)D_t)dt+\sqrt8\,dB_t,
 \qquad dE_t=-4E_tdt+\sqrt8\,dB'_t, \tag{15}
\]
with independent initial coordinates and independent Brownian noises.

Let \(H=\inf\{t:\|D_t\|^2\le a\}\).  On \((a,\infty)\), It\^o's formula applied to \(R_t=\|D_t\|^2\) gives
\[
 dR_t=8(k-2\gamma-R_t)dt+\sqrt{32R_t}\,d\beta_t. \tag{16}
\]
A scale derivative for (16) is
\[
 s'(r)=e^{r/2}r^{\gamma-k/2}.
\]
Indeed substitution in the one-dimensional generator gives \(\mathcal L_Rs=0\).  Optional stopping of \(s(R_t)\) on exit from \([a,M]\) gives
\[
 \Pr_r(T_M<T_a)=\frac{s(r)-s(a)}{s(M)-s(a)}.
\]
Because \(\int^M e^{y/2}y^{\gamma-k/2}dy\to\infty\), the right side tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\).  On every compact interval above \(a>0\), the diffusion coefficient is bounded away from zero and the expected exit time is finite by applying the generator to the solution of the corresponding bounded Dirichlet problem.  Therefore \(H<\infty\) almost surely from every finite exterior point; it is zero from an interior point.

The Gaussian initialization puts zero mass on \(\{\|D_0\|^2=a\}\).  At the hit from outside, the radial diffusion coefficient in (16) equals \(\sqrt{32a}>0\).  The time-changed Brownian martingale therefore visits both sides of its hit level arbitrarily soon, while its finite-variation drift is of smaller local order.  Thus the limiting path enters the strict interior immediately after its first boundary hit.  These facts are exactly the continuity conditions for the closed-ball first-hit map: strict initial interior points have hit time zero stably, and exterior paths have a finite hit followed immediately by an interior crossing.  The maximal-jump terminal estimate in the resolved characteristic theorem supplies the discrete crossing condition.

Applying the continuous mapping argument on \([0,L]\) gives joint convergence of the stopped path and \(T_n/n\) on \(\{H\le L\}\).  Letting \(L\to\infty\) is valid because \(H<\infty\) almost surely; it also proves \(T_n/n=O_{\Pr}(1)\).  Since \(\phi'(r)=1/r\) for \(r\ge a/2\), (15) before \(H\) is exactly the diffusion in the limit-system definition.  Absorption at \(H\) finally yields
\[
 (\bar Z_n,T_n/n)\Rightarrow(((D_{t\wedge H}^{\mathsf T},E_{t\wedge H})^{\mathsf T})_{t\ge0},H),
\]
as claimed.

The functional-limit theorem gives convergence of the terminal coordinates to \((D_H,E_H)\).  On \(\{\|G\|^2\le a\}\), one has \(H=0\) and hence \(D_H=G\).  On the complementary event, path continuity gives \(\|D_H\|=\sqrt a\).

The covariate equation is equivariant under every orthogonal transformation, its Gaussian initial law is rotationally invariant, and the first-hit rule depends only on radius.  Consequently the conditional distribution of \(D_H/\sqrt a\) on \(\{\|G\|^2>a\}\) is the uniform distribution on the unit sphere.  The event defining this branch has probability \(\Pr(\|G\|^2>a)\).  Thus the endpoint law consists of the unaltered Gaussian mass inside the ball and a uniform spherical mass of exactly the Gaussian exterior probability on its boundary.  This is precisely
\[
 D_H\overset d=G\min\{1,\sqrt a/\|G\|\}=C_{k,a}. \tag{17}
\]
This argument uses only rotational equivariance; although the endpoint direction is uniform, it need not equal the initial direction pathwise.

The residual equation has the explicit solution
\[
 E_t=e^{-4t}\varepsilon+\sqrt8\int_0^te^{-4(t-u)}\,dB'_u.
\]
It is stationary standard Gaussian because its variance is \(e^{-8t}+8\int_0^te^{-8(t-u)}du=1\).  The entire residual process is independent of the entire covariate process, while \(H\) is measurable with respect to the latter.  Hence, for bounded measurable \(f\) and every bounded covariate-path functional \(A\), conditioning on the covariate path gives
\[
 \mathbb E\{f(E_H)A(D)\}=\mathbb E\{f(\varepsilon)\}\mathbb E\{A(D)\}. \tag{18}
\]
Therefore \(E_H\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and is independent of \(D_H\), despite the absence of any finite-population outcome--residual independence assumption.

Equation (17) implies
\[
 \|C_{k,a}\|^2=\min\{\|G\|^2,a\}=\min\{\chi_k^2,a\},
\]
so the boundary mass is \(1-\Pr(\chi_k^2\le a)>0\).  Neither (17) nor (18) contains \(\gamma\).  In contrast, the radial drift in (16) contains \(-16\gamma\), so the law of \(H\) may depend on tuning.  This proves both the tuning-sensitive search clock and the tuning-insensitive first-order terminal law.

By the clipped-Gaussian definition,
\[
 \Pr\{\|C_{k,a}\|^2=a\}=\Pr\{\|G\|^2\ge a\}=1-\Pr(\chi_k^2\le a)>0,
\]
where equality or strict inequality at \(a\) is immaterial because the chi-square distribution is continuous.  By contrast,
\[
 L_{k,a}\overset d=G\mid\{\|G\|^2\le a\}.
\]
The conditional radial distribution is the continuous chi-square law restricted to \([0,a]\), and therefore
\[
 \Pr\{\|L_{k,a}\|^2=a\}=0.
\]
The two probability laws assign different probabilities to the measurable sphere \(\{d:\|d\|^2=a\}\), so they cannot be equal.  This boundary-atom certificate concerns every finite \(a>0\) and directly rules out replacing first-entry PSRR by a uniform acceptable-set draw.

The exact identity in the initialization lemma is
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)
 =b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})+s_nE_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}). \tag{19}
\]
The radial-entrance theorem gives joint convergence of the two random coordinates to independent \((C_{k,a},\varepsilon)\).  The hypotheses \(b_n\to b\) and \(s_n\to s>0\) are deterministic.  Applying the continuous mapping theorem to (19), followed by deterministic Slutsky convergence, gives
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)\Rightarrow b^{\mathsf T}C_{k,a}+s\varepsilon,
\]
with \(C_{k,a}\perp\varepsilon\).  The target remains the fixed finite-population causal contrast \(\tau_n\); the right side is its design-randomization limit, not a redefinition of the estimand.

The joint functional-limit theorem implies \(T_n/n=O_{\Pr}(1)\).  Fix \(\eta>0\).  Choose \(L<\infty\) such that \(\limsup_n\Pr(T_n>nL)<\eta\).  Apply actual-path arm uniformity to the finite collection of bounded deterministic arrays
\[
 1,\quad x_{nij},\quad x_{nij}x_{ni\ell},\quad Y_{ni}(z),\quad
 x_{nij}Y_{ni}(z),\quad Y_{ni}(z)^2,
 \qquad z\in\{0,1\},\ 1\le j,\ell\le k. \tag{20}
\]
Uniform boundedness verifies the envelope condition.  On \(\{T_n\le nL\}\), every treated- and control-arm raw empirical moment in (20), evaluated at \(T_n\), differs from its full-population counterpart by \(o_{\Pr}(1)\).  The probability of the complement is at most \(\eta+o(1)\); letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) proves the same statement unconditionally.

Centered covariances are polynomial functions of these raw moments, so the observed arm covariance and outcome--covariate vectors differ from \(S_{xx,n}\) and \(S_{x,Y(z),n}\) by \(o_{\Pr}(1)\), with the immaterial divisor corrections also \(o(1)\).  Since \(\lambda_{\min}(S_{xx,n})\ge c_x/2\), eigenvalue continuity implies that both observed arm Gram matrices are nonsingular with probability tending to one, and their inverses differ from \(S_{xx,n}^{-1}\) by \(o_{\Pr}(1)\).  Thus the Moore--Penrose convention on the vanishing singular event has no first-order effect.

The same continuous algebra gives, row by row,
\[
 \widehat c_{z,n}-S_{x,Y(z),n}=o_{\Pr}(1),\qquad
 \widehat S_{e_z,n}^2-S_{e_ze_z,n}=o_{\Pr}(1). \tag{21}
\]
The inverse square roots of \(S_{xx,n}\) are uniformly bounded, so the definitions and (21) yield
\[
 \widehat b_n-b_n
 =S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}\{(\widehat c_{1,n}-S_{x,Y(1),n})+(\widehat c_{0,n}-S_{x,Y(0),n})\}
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0,
\]
and
\[
 \widehat u_n-u_n
 =2(\widehat S_{e_1,n}^2-S_{e_1e_1,n})+2(\widehat S_{e_0,n}^2-S_{e_0e_0,n})
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0.
\]
This proves stopped-design consistency without conditioning the terminal allocation on uniform acceptance.

Fix an arbitrary sequence in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}\); all probabilities below are over assignment only, because the potential outcomes are fixed.  Second-moment convergence and the uniform positive-definiteness of \(S_{xx,n}\) imply convergence of \(S_{xx,n}^{-1}\), the arm slopes, and all residual second moments.  Write
\[
 b_n\to b,\qquad s_n^2\to s^2>0,\qquad u_n\to u.
\]
The residual identities in the variance-envelope definition give exactly
\[
 s_n^2=S_{e_1+e_0,e_1+e_0,n},\qquad
 u_n-s_n^2=S_{e_1-e_0,e_1-e_0,n}\ge0, \tag{22}
\]
and hence \(0<s^2\le u\).  This is an upper envelope, not identification of the unobserved residual treatment-effect variance.

We next establish existence and computability of the critical value.  Let \(R=\|G\|\) and \(U=G/\|G\|\), with an arbitrary value at \(G=0\).  Then \(R\sim\chi_k\), \(U\) is uniform on the unit sphere, and they are independent.  Therefore
\[
 (C_{k,a})_1=\min(R,\sqrt a)U_1. \tag{23}
\]
For \(v>0\), the distribution function of
\(X_{v,B}=|\sqrt v\,\varepsilon+B(C_{k,a})_1|\) is the explicit integral
\[
 F_{v,B}(t)=\mathbb E_{R,U}\left[
 \Phi\left(\frac{t-B\min(R,\sqrt a)U_1}{\sqrt v}\right)
 -\Phi\left(\frac{-t-B\min(R,\sqrt a)U_1}{\sqrt v}\right)
 \right]. \tag{24}
\]
For \(k\ge2\), \(U_1\) has density
\[
 c_k(1-u^2)^{(k-3)/2}\mathbf1_{(-1,1)}(u),
 \qquad c_k=\frac{\Gamma(k/2)}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma((k-1)/2)},
\]
and for \(k=1\) it is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\).  Together with the chi density for \(R\), (24) is the asserted Gaussian--spherical integral.  At \(v=0\), the same formula is interpreted as the indicator integral from (23).  Bisection in \(t\), numerical quadrature in \((R,U_1)\), and one-dimensional maximization in \(v\) approximate the answer to arbitrary prescribed accuracy.

For completeness, the maximum is attained.  Couple all \(X_{v,B}\)'s using the same \((\varepsilon,C_{k,a})\).  If \((v_j,B_j)\to(v,B)\), then \(X_{v_j,B_j}\to X_{v,B}\) almost surely.  When \(v>0\), convolution with the Gaussian gives a continuous positive density.  When \(v=0<B\), (23) has positive density throughout the interior of its support; for \(k=1\) it may additionally have an endpoint atom, but there is no gap below that endpoint.  Consequently, if \(q=q_\alpha(v,B)\), then for every \(\delta>0\),
\[
 F_{v,B}((q-\delta)_+)<1-\alpha<F_{v,B}(q+\delta), \tag{25}
\]
with the left inequality omitted when \(q=0\).  Almost-sure coupling and (25) imply \(q_\alpha(v_j,B_j)\to q_\alpha(v,B)\).  At \((v,B)=(0,0)\), continuity follows directly from
\[
 q_\alpha(v,B)\le B\sqrt a+\sqrt v\,q_\alpha(1,0).
\]
Thus \((v,B)\mapsto q_\alpha(v,B)\) is continuous.  Reparameterize \(v=ut\), \(t\in[0,1]\).  Continuity on the compact set in \(t\) proves that
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,B)=\max_{t\in[0,1]}q_\alpha(ut,B) \tag{26}
\]
exists.  The same compactness argument applied to maximizing subsequences proves continuity of \(q_{*,\alpha}\) in \((u,B)\).

Stopped-moment consistency and (26) now give
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(\widehat u_n,\|\widehat b_n\|)
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}q_{*,\alpha}(u,\|b\|). \tag{27}
\]
Rotational invariance yields \(b^{\mathsf T}C_{k,a}\overset d=\|b\|(C_{k,a})_1\).  By (22) and the definition of the maximum,
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,\|b\|)\ge q_\alpha(s^2,\|b\|). \tag{28}
\]
The ATE limit and \(s>0\) show that the limiting absolute error has a continuous distribution.  Combining (27)--(28) with Slutsky's theorem gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr(\tau_n\in I_n)
 &=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr\left\{\left|\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)\right|
 \le q_{*,\alpha}(\widehat u_n,\|\widehat b_n\|)\right\}\\
 &\ge1-\alpha.
 \end{split}
\]

An exact four-unit check also confirms why the conclusion is only asymptotic.  Take \(k=1\), \(a=1\), \(x=(-3,-1,1,3)\), \(Y(0)=0\), and \(Y(1)=(1,1,1,-3)\).  Here \(S_{xx}=20/3\).  Of the six balanced allocations, the four whose treated covariate sums are \(0\) or \(\pm2\) are acceptable, while the two with sums \(\pm4\) enter the acceptable set after one proposal.  Enumeration shows that the four terminal allocations each have probability \(1/4\), for every finite \(\gamma\).  The ATE is zero.  On each of the two terminal allocations selecting two equal treated outcomes, intercept-plus-slope OLS has \(\widehat u=0\) and \(\widehat b=0\), so the reported interval is the singleton \(\{1\}\), which misses zero.  Thus at \(\alpha=0.05\) finite-sample coverage is at most \(1/2\).  This stress test refutes finite-sample exactness but is fully consistent with the proved sequencewise asymptotic guarantee.

Let \(\widehat\beta_{z,n}\) be the within-arm OLS slope.  Because the population covariates are centered and the arms are equal, \(\bar x_{1,n}+\bar x_{0,n}=0\).  The coefficient on treatment in the fully interacted regression is the difference of the two fitted intercepts, so the identity
\[
 \widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}
 =\widehat\tau_n-\frac12(\widehat\beta_{1,n}+\widehat\beta_{0,n})^{\mathsf T}
 (\bar x_{1,n}-\bar x_{0,n}) \tag{29}
\]
holds whenever the arm Gram matrices are nonsingular; the Moore--Penrose version agrees asymptotically because singularity has probability tending to zero.  Stopped-moment consistency gives \(\widehat\beta_{z,n}-\beta_{z,n}=o_{\Pr}(1)\).  Moreover, directly from the score definition,
\[
 \bar x_{1,n}-\bar x_{0,n}=\frac2{\sqrt n}S_{xx,n}^{1/2}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}),
 \qquad S_{xx,n}^{1/2}(\beta_{1,n}+\beta_{0,n})=b_n. \tag{30}
\]
Since \(\|D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})\|\le\sqrt a\), (29)--(30) and the exact ATE decomposition imply
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}-\tau_n)
 =b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n+s_nE_n-b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n+o_{\Pr}(1)
 =s_nE_n+o_{\Pr}(1). \tag{31}
\]
The radial-entrance theorem and \(s_n\to s>0\) therefore give the asserted \(\mathcal N(0,s^2)\) limit.

Let \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) be the standard-normal two-sided critical value.  The residual-Neyman interval has half-width \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat u_n/n}\).  By stopped-moment consistency, \(\widehat u_n\to_{\Pr}u\), while the variance identity gives \(u\ge s^2\).  From (31),
\[
 \liminf_n\Pr\left\{\left|\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}-\tau_n)\right|
 \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat u_n}\right\}
 \ge1-\alpha.
\]
If \(u_n-s_n^2\to0\), then \(u=s^2\), and the limiting standardized statistic is exactly standard normal; continuity of the Gaussian distribution makes the limiting coverage exactly \(1-\alpha\).

If \(b=0\), the ATE limit reduces immediately to \(s\varepsilon\), hence to \(\mathcal N(0,s^2)\).  When \(B_0=0\), the clipped-Gaussian term in the critical-value definition vanishes, so for every \(v\ge0\),
\[
 q_\alpha(v,0)=\sqrt v\,c_\alpha,
 \qquad c_\alpha=\inf\{t\ge0:\Pr(|\varepsilon|\le t)\ge1-\alpha\}.
\]
The right side is nondecreasing in \(v\).  Maximizing over \(0\le v\le u\) therefore gives
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,0)=\sqrt u\,c_\alpha,
\]
including \(u=0\).  Substitution in the interval definition is exactly the usual conservative Neyman Gaussian half-width \(c_\alpha\sqrt{u/n}\), with \(u\) replaced by its consistent observable envelope.  This is a consequence of the stopped-design law, not an assumption of complete randomization.

theorem.statement:
The answer is affirmative along the actual uniformly initialized path, but not uniformly over arbitrary balanced states.  For every fixed \(L,R<\infty\), with \(Z_{n,m}=Z_n(W_{n,m})=(D_{n,m}^{\mathsf T},E_{n,m})^{\mathsf T}\),
\[
 \max_{\substack{0\le m<\lfloor nL\rfloor\wedge T_n\\ \|Z_{n,m}\|\le R}}
 \left\|n\mathbb E(\Delta Z_{n,m}\mid\mathcal F_{n,m})+4Z_{n,m}
 +\frac{8\gamma}{\|D_{n,m}\|^2}(D_{n,m}^{\mathsf T},0)^{\mathsf T}\right\|\longrightarrow_{\Pr}0,
\]
\[
 \max_{\substack{0\le m<\lfloor nL\rfloor\wedge T_n\\ \|Z_{n,m}\|\le R}}
 \left\|n\mathbb E(\Delta Z_{n,m}\Delta Z_{n,m}^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_{n,m})-8I_{k+1}\right\|\longrightarrow_{\Pr}0.
\]
For every \(\eta>0\), the analogous maximum of
\(n\mathbb E[\|\Delta Z_{n,m}\|^2\mathbf 1\{\|\Delta Z_{n,m}\|>\eta\}\mid\mathcal F_{n,m}]\) is eventually zero.  If \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) is smooth, constant near zero, and equals \(\log m\) for \(m\ge a/2\), the corresponding smooth extension has localized characteristics with the singular factor \(D/\|D\|^2\) replaced by the globally smooth factor \(\phi'(\|D\|^2)D\).  It agrees with original PSRR before first entry.  On \(\{T_n>0\}\), the exact terminal transposition and the maximal score bound give
\[
 \operatorname{dist}\bigl(D_n(W_{n,T_n}),\{d:\|d\|^2=a\}\bigr)\longrightarrow_{\Pr}0.
\]
Thus the terminal crossing can be transferred separately, without evaluating the singular drift at or after \(T_n\).  No projected Markov property, stabilization, outcome--residual independence assumption, or empirical-law limit is used.
theorem.proof_tex:
Write \(q_i=q_{ni}\), \(Z=Z_n(W_{n,m})=(D^{\mathsf T},E)^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(i\) and \(j\) be respectively the uniformly selected treated and control indices.  Before the acceptance decision the proposed score increment is
\[
 \delta=\frac2{\sqrt n}(q_j-q_i).
\]
Since \(\sum_iq_i=0\), the treated and control score means are \(Z/\sqrt n\) and \(-Z/\sqrt n\).  Direct expansion therefore gives, at every balanced state,
\[
 \mathbb E(\delta\mid W)=-\frac4nZ,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E(\delta\delta^{\mathsf T}\mid W)
 =\frac{8(n-1)}{n^2}I_{k+1}+\frac8{n^2}ZZ^{\mathsf T}. \tag{5}
\]

On the localized pre-entry set, \(\|D\|^2>a\) and \(\|Z\|\le R\).  Taylor expansion of the exact Metropolis probability, uniformly on this set, yields
\[
 A=1-\frac{2\gamma}{\|D\|^2}(D^{\mathsf T}\delta_D)_++O(n^{-1}). \tag{6}
\]
Acceptance randomness is conditionally independent after the proposal, so the conditional drift is \(\mathbb E(A\delta\mid W)\).  Using \(x_+=(x+|x|)/2\), (5), and (6),
\[
 \begin{split}
 n\mathbb E(A\delta\mid W)
 ={}&-4Z-\frac{\gamma n}{\|D\|^2}\mathbb E(\delta\delta_D^{\mathsf T}\mid W)D\\
 &-\frac{\gamma n}{\|D\|^2}\mathbb E\{\delta|D^{\mathsf T}\delta_D|\mid W\}+O(n^{-1/2}). \tag{7}
 \end{split}
\]
The middle term in (7) is \(-8\gamma(D^{\mathsf T},0)^{\mathsf T}/\|D\|^2+o(1)\), uniformly on the localized path, by (5).  It remains to control the kink term; projection orthogonality alone is not enough.

Let \(\nu_T,\nu_C\) be the two arm empirical probability measures on the \(q_i\)'s, let \(\mu=(\nu_T+\nu_C)/2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{q_i}\), and put \(\xi=(\nu_T-\nu_C)/2\).  For a unit vector \(u\in\mathbb R^k\) and coordinate \(\ell\le k+1\), define
\[
 F_{u,\ell}(q,q')=(q'_\ell-q_\ell)|u^{\mathsf T}(q'_D-q_D)|,
 \qquad g_{n,u,\ell}(q)=\int F_{u,\ell}(q,q')\,\mu(dq').
\]
The kernel is antisymmetric.  Hence its integrals against \(\mu\otimes\mu\) and \(\xi\otimes\xi\) vanish, the two mixed terms agree, and \(\int g_{n,u,\ell}\,d\mu=0\).  Thus the exact identity
\[
 \iint F_{u,\ell}(q,q')\,\nu_T(dq)\nu_C(dq')
 =2\int g_{n,u,\ell}(q)\,\nu_T(dq) \tag{8}
\]
holds for every row and state.  The functions on the right are deterministic, uniformly bounded, and uniformly Lipschitz in \(u\), because \(q_i\) are uniformly bounded.  Actual-path arm uniformity, with the unit sphere as parameter set, makes (8) \(o_{\Pr}(1)\) uniformly through \(nL\) proposals.  Taking \(u=D/\|D\|\) shows that the last expectation in (7), after multiplication by \(n\), is \(o_{\Pr}(1)\).  This proves the drift assertion.

The same expansion gives \(1-A=O(n^{-1/2})\) locally.  Since \(\|\delta\|=O(n^{-1/2})\),
\[
 n\left\|\mathbb E\{(1-A)\delta\delta^{\mathsf T}\mid W\}\right\|=O(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Combining this with (5) proves the second-characteristic assertion, including the vanishing covariate--residual cross-characteristics.  The deterministic jump bound makes the displayed conditional Lindeberg term zero for all sufficiently large \(n\).

The necessity of the actual-path qualification is witnessed exactly at \(a=1\).  Take six score pairs with covariate coordinates
\[
 (-2,0,2,-1,-1,2)
\]
and residual coordinates \((1,-2,1,0,0,0)\), treating the first three.  Both arm means and the population covariate--residual covariance are zero, but direct summation over the nine ordered treated--control pairs gives
\[
 \frac19\sum_{i\in T,j\in C}(r_j-r_i)|x_j-x_i|=\frac{-6+8-6}{9}=-\frac49. \tag{9}
\]
Repeating the six types and changing only \(O(\sqrt n)\) labels produces bounded exterior projected scores while preserving the limit in (9).  Thus an order-one erroneous kink drift would remain at both \(\gamma=1\) and \(\gamma=10\) if one asserted uniformity over all balanced states.  The coupling and (8) show that these states are not representative of the uniformly initialized actual path; no additional initialization or empirical-distribution assumption is needed.

For the smooth extension in the coupling lemma the identical computation uses
\(A=1-2\gamma\phi'(\|D\|^2)(D^{\mathsf T}\delta_D)_++O(n^{-1})\).  It gives drift \(-4Z-8\gamma\phi'(\|D\|^2)(D^{\mathsf T},0)^{\mathsf T}\) and covariance \(8I_{k+1}\).  Before entry, \(\phi'(\|D\|^2)=1/\|D\|^2\).

Finally, on \(\{T_n>0\}\), \(\|D_{n,T_n-1}\|>\sqrt a\), \(\|D_{n,T_n}\|\le\sqrt a\), and a transposition changes \(D\) by at most \(4C/\sqrt n\).  Hence
\[
 0\le\sqrt a-\|D_{n,T_n}\|\le4C/\sqrt n.
\]
This is the promised separate crossing control and never evaluates \(D/\|D\|^2\) at the stopped state.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(q_{ni}\in\mathbb R^p\), where \(p\) is fixed, be a deterministic triangular array satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^n q_{ni}=0\), \((n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nq_{ni}q_{ni}^{\mathsf T}\to\Sigma\), and \(n^{-1}\max_{i\le n}\|q_{ni}\|^2\to0\).  If \(W_{n,0}\) is uniform on the balanced allocation space, then
\[
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(2W_{n,0,i}-1)q_{ni}\Rightarrow\mathcal N_p(0,\Sigma).
\]

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be smooth, constant near zero, and equal to \(\log m\) for \(m\ge a/2\).  Extend each transition by using acceptance \(1\wedge\exp[-\gamma\{\phi(\|D^*\|^2)-\phi(\|D\|^2)\}]\), and implement this extension at an all-pairs clock, with same-label pairs acting as identity moves.  There is a coupling of this extension with a stationary uniform balanced-allocation shadow \((V_{n,\ell})_{\ell\ge0}\) such that, for every fixed \(L<\infty\),
\[
 \max_{0\le\ell\le\lfloor nL\rfloor}d_H(\widetilde W_{n,\ell},V_{n,\ell})=O_{\Pr}(\sqrt n).
\]
The indicator that an all-pairs tick selects opposite labels is an independent Bernoulli variable with success probability \(p_n^{\mathrm{op}}=n/[2(n-1)]\).  If \(A_n(m)\) is the number of all-pairs ticks needed to obtain \(m\) opposite-label proposals, then, for every fixed \(L\),
\[
 \max_{0\le m\le\lfloor nL\rfloor}\left|\frac{A_n(m)}n-\frac{m}{np_n^{\mathrm{op}}}\right|\longrightarrow_{\Pr}0.
\]
Deleting same-label ticks therefore recovers the original proposal clock, and the factor \((p_n^{\mathrm{op}})^{-1}\to2\) converts the all-pairs characteristics to the original proposal-time characteristics.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
On the retained tail the score bound established in the initialization proof gives \(\max_i\|q_{ni}\|\le C\).  Hence every transposition changes \(Z_n\) by at most \(4C/\sqrt n\).  Choose a smooth \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) which is constant near zero, equals \(\log m\) for \(m\ge a/2\), and has bounded first two derivatives after composition with \(d\mapsto\|d\|^2\).  Put \(U(d)=\phi(\|d\|^2)\), and extend the transition rule by accepting a proposed transposition with probability
\[
 A_n(d,d^*)=1\wedge\exp\{-\gamma(U(d^*)-U(d))\}. \tag{2}
\]
The radial change in one proposal is at most \(4C/\sqrt n\).  Thus, for all sufficiently large \(n\), a proposal from \(\|d\|^2>a\) cannot land in \(\|d^*\|^2<a/2\), so (2) agrees exactly with original PSRR up to first entry.

At each auxiliary tick choose an unordered pair uniformly from the \(n(n-1)/2\) pairs.  The process \(\widetilde W\) applies (2) when the labels are opposite and regards a same-label transposition as an identity move.  Start \(V_{n,0}=\widetilde W_{n,0}\), and at every tick transpose the same two coordinates of \(V\), without rejection.  A common transposition preserves Hamming distance, including when the two labels of \(\widetilde W\) agree, because then that coordinate permutation fixes \(\widetilde W\).  A rejection can increase Hamming distance by at most two.  Since \(U\) is globally Lipschitz and a score jump is \(O(n^{-1/2})\),
\[
 1-A_n(d,d^*)\le\gamma|U(d^*)-U(d)|\le C_1n^{-1/2}. \tag{3}
\]
If \(R_n(L)\) counts rejections through \(\lfloor nL\rfloor\) ticks, then (3) gives \(\mathbb E R_n(L)\le C_1L\sqrt n\).  Markov's inequality and
\[
 \max_{\ell\le nL}d_H(\widetilde W_{n,\ell},V_{n,\ell})\le2R_n(L)
\]
prove the first assertion.  The shadow starts uniformly and each tick applies a coordinate permutation independent of its current value, so its uniform balanced law is stationary at every tick; no mixing assertion is being used.

Given the past, exactly \((n/2)^2\) unordered pairs have opposite labels.  Hence the opposite-label indicator \(J_{n,\ell}\) has the state-independent conditional probability
\[
 p_n^{\mathrm{op}}=\frac{n^2/4}{n(n-1)/2}=\frac{n}{2(n-1)}.
\]
The constancy of this conditional law shows inductively that the indicators are independent Bernoulli variables.  For \(S_n(r)=\sum_{\ell<r}(J_{n,\ell}-p_n^{\mathrm{op}})\), the elementary maximal second-moment inequality gives, for fixed \(C_2\),
\[
 \Pr\left\{\max_{r\le C_2n}|S_n(r)|>\eta n\right\}
 \le \frac{C_2n p_n^{\mathrm{op}}(1-p_n^{\mathrm{op}})}{\eta^2n^2}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Monotone inversion of the counting process yields the displayed uniform inverse-clock relation.  Conditional on \(J_{n,\ell}=1\), the chosen pair is uniform among the treated--control pairs, so deleting the zeros produces exactly the original proposal chain, including its Metropolis rejection self-loops.  This proves the clock conversion and not a modified algorithm.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(A_{ni}=(x_{ni}^{\mathsf T},Y_{ni}(0),Y_{ni}(1))^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(\{f_{n,\vartheta}:\vartheta\in\Theta\}\) be any deterministic family evaluated on these records (or on the derived scores \(q_{ni}\)), where \(\Theta\) is a compact subset of a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space, \(\sup_{n,i,\vartheta}|f_{n,\vartheta}(A_{ni})|<\infty\), and
\[
 \sup_{n,i}|f_{n,\vartheta}(A_{ni})-f_{n,\vartheta'}(A_{ni})|\le C\|\vartheta-\vartheta'\|.
\]
Then, for every fixed \(L<\infty\), along the actual original-PSRR path,
\[
 \sup_{\vartheta\in\Theta}\max_{0\le m\le\lfloor nL\rfloor\wedge T_n}
 \left|\frac2n\sum_{i:W_{n,m,i}=1}f_{n,\vartheta}(A_{ni})-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf_{n,\vartheta}(A_{ni})\right|
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0,
\]
and the analogous control-arm assertion holds.  The conclusion requires no convergence of the population empirical distribution.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
First work at the auxiliary all-pairs clock.  At every fixed tick \(\ell\), stationarity of the shadow makes \(\{i:V_{n,\ell,i}=1\}\) a uniform subset of size \(n/2\).  If \(|f_i|\le C_0\), exposing a uniform random permutation one coordinate at a time and applying the exponential-moment argument for its bounded martingale differences gives
\[
 \Pr\left(\left|\frac2n\sum_{i:V_{n,\ell,i}=1}f_i-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf_i\right|>\eta\right)
 \le2\exp(-c n\eta^2/C_0^2) \tag{4}
\]
for a universal \(c>0\).  This derivation uses only sampling without replacement and does not require independence across ticks.

For a mesh of size \(n^{-2}\), compactness in fixed dimension supplies a net \(\Theta_n\) of polynomial cardinality.  Take \(\eta_n=A\sqrt{\log n/n}\) with \(A\) large enough.  A union bound in (4) over \(\ell\le nL\) and \(\vartheta\in\Theta_n\) tends to zero.  Lipschitz interpolation from the net then shows that the displayed deviation for the shadow is \(O_{\Pr}(\sqrt{\log n/n})\), uniformly in both arguments.

Changing one treatment label changes a normalized arm sum by at most \(2C_0/n\).  The coupling lemma consequently gives
\[
 \max_{\ell\le nL}\sup_{\vartheta\in\Theta}
 \left|\frac2n\sum_{i:\widetilde W_{n,\ell,i}=1}f_{n,\vartheta}(A_{ni})
 -\frac2n\sum_{i:V_{n,\ell,i}=1}f_{n,\vartheta}(A_{ni})\right|
 \le \frac{2C_0}{n}\max_{\ell\le nL}d_H(\widetilde W_{n,\ell},V_{n,\ell})
 =O_{\Pr}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Thus the all-pairs extension has the asserted uniformity.  The inverse-clock relation transfers it to every original proposal time up to \(nL\); before \(T_n\) the smooth extension and original PSRR coincide.  Finally, equal allocation and the identity that the two arm empirical measures average to the population empirical measure give the control-arm assertion.  The proof is rowwise and nowhere takes a limit of the empirical distribution.

proposed.statement: The index \(N_0\) in the deterministic regular-tail definition is finite.  More precisely, on the eventual positive-definite covariance tail, the finite-population Gaussian initialization gives \(D_n(W_{n,0})\Rightarrow G\) and hence \(p_n=\Pr\{M_n(W_{n,0})\le a\}\to\Pr(\|G\|^2\le a)>0\).  Therefore \(\mathcal A_n(a)\ne\varnothing\), \(S_{xx,n}\) is positive definite, and \(s_n=\sqrt{v_n}>0\) for every even \(n\ge N_0\).  Because the balanced pair-swap graph is finite and connected and every required transition has positive probability for finite \(\gamma\), \(T_n<\infty\) almost surely on this retained tail; the discarded rows \(n<N_0\) have no asymptotic role.

Along the retained even tail \(n\ge N_0\), if \(b=0\), then \(\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,s^2)\).  For every \(u\ge0\),
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,0)=\sqrt u\inf\{t\ge0:\Pr(|\varepsilon|\le t)\ge1-\alpha\},
\]
so the envelope interval reduces to the standard conservative Neyman Gaussian form.
